BACKGROUND

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a Hearings Customer
Service Representative GS-8, at the Agency’s Hearing Office in Kansas City, Missouri.

On May 17, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency discriminated
against her on the bases of age, disability, and reprisal for prior protected EEO activity when:

1. From February 16, 2021, and continuing, the Supervisor subject ed Complainant
to harassment by giving her an overwhelming number of daily work assignments,
and daily reviews of her performance.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2022001628

2
2. On March 12, 2021, the Supervisor placed Complainant on an Opportunity to
Perform Successfully (OPS).

3. On February 16, 2021, Complainant was required to resume performance of the
Verbatim Hearing Reporter (VHR) duties from which she had been exempted.

Furthermore, on the face of her formal complaint, Complainant alleged that she had received
“threats of termination,” and that management had done “any and everything within their power
to force [her] into retirement. ” In an attachment to her complaint, she reiterated “management
staff has left me with no other recourse, other than to concede to being forced out of my position
and into retirement!”

On June 22, 2021, the Supervisor issued a Proposal to Terminate to Complainant, notifying her
that her employment would be terminated within 30 days of receipt o f the Proposal . The
Proposal to Terminate described that C omplainant’s performance was unacceptable and that the
Supervisor tried to assist Complainant improve her performance by giving her a “fair share” of
daily work assignments (claim 1) and placing her on an OPS plan (claim 2). Believing that was
being forced to retire, Complainant submitted retirement paperwork on July 27, 2021.

On August 2, 2021, the Agency began its EEO investigation into the formal complaint.
Complainant informed the investigator that she had received a Proposal to Terminate , and that
she believed the Su pervisor had “set her up” for “forced ” retirement by giving her an
“overwhelming [number of] daily tasks” (claim 1) and placing her on an OPS plan (claim 2).

By memorandum dated August 6, 2021, the Supervisor notified C omplainant that he had made
the decision to terminate her employment with the Agency effective August 6, 2021. However,
the Supervisor sent Complainant an email afterward to inform her that he rescinded his decision
because she filed r etirement pape rwork in July. Complainant’s representative forwarded the
memorandum and email to the investigator and reiterated that the Agency’s actions had “forced”
Complainant into “involuntary retirement.”

The investigation was concluded on October 1, 2021. There is no indication in the record that the
Agency accepted Complainant’s constructive discharge claim as part of her original complaint or
as an amendment to it. Therefore, it does not appear as part of the report of investigation.

The Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the re port of investig ation and notice of her
right to request a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did
not request an EEOC hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the
Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) , with appeal rights to this
Commission. The decision concluded that no discrimination was established as alleged . The
Agency’s final decision did not address Complainant’s constructive discharge claim.

Complainant appealed the Agency’s decision to the Commission. She did not submit a brief or
statement with her appeal.

2022001628

3
ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Although Complainant’s retirement from the Agency was not effective at the time she filed her
formal EEO complaint, on the face of that complaint, Complainant alleged that she had received
“threats of termination,” and that management had done “any and everything within their power
to force [her] into retirement. ” In an attachment to her complaint, she reiterated “management
staff has left me with no other recourse, other than to concede to being forced out of my position
and into retirement! ” Once the Agency ’s investigation of her complaint was underway,
Complainant notified the investigator that she had been served with a notice of proposed removal
and that she believed she was being set up for a “ forced retirement.” The record shows that the
proposal to remove Complainant was rescinded once she initiated the retirement process.
However, despite Complainant’s repeated and clear allegations of a discriminatory constructive
discharge, the Agency did not accept the claim as an amendmen t to her original complaint , did
not investigate the claim , and did not address it in its final decision. The Agency erred in not
doing so. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.106(d) provides that a complainant may amend a complaint at any
time prior to the conclusion of the inves tigation to include issues or claims like or related to
those raised in the complaint. Here, the constructive discharge claim, which Complainant
expressly raised during the EEO investigation, was clearly like or re lated to the issues raised in
her original complaint and should have been accepted by the Agency as an amendment and
investigated.
Inasmuch as the Agency did not properly process Complainant’s complaint, the Commission has
determined that the final agency decision should be vacated, and the c omplaint should be
remanded to the A gency for a supplemental investigation on the constructive discharge claim
and issuance of a new final agency decision with appropriate appeal rights. In doing so, we note
that the constructive discharge claim is most likely a “mixed case complaint” claim stemming
from an action that is appealable to the Merit Systems Protection Board (M SPB). See 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.302(a)(1). Issues concerning termination and discharge, including allegations of
constructive discharge, are matters ordinarily under the jurisdiction of the MSPB. See DeMuse v.
United States Postal Service, EEOC Request No. 01950324. Therefore, the Agency should
include appeal rights to the MSPB when it issues its new final decision on this matter.

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, the Agency’s final decision is VACATED and the complaint is
REMANDED for further processing in accordance with the Order below.

ORDER

The Agency is ordered to take the following actions:

1. The Agency shall ensure that its investigator completes a supplemental investigation into
the constructive discharge claim within ninety (90) calendar days of the date this decision

is issued. The supplem ental investigation shall include affidavits fro m Complainant and

2. On March 12, 2021, the Supervisor placed Complainant on an Opportunity to

Furthermore, on the face of her formal complaint, Complainant alleged that she had received
“threats of termination,” and that management had done “any and everything within their power
to force [her] into retirement. ” In an attachment to her complaint, she reiterated “management
staff has left me with no other recourse, other than to concede to being forced out of my position
and into retirement!”

On June 22, 2021, the Supervisor issued a Proposal to Terminate to Complainant, notifying her
that her employment would be terminated within 30 days of receipt o f the Proposal . The
Proposal to Terminate described that C omplainant’s performance was unacceptable and that the
Supervisor tried to assist Complainant improve her performance by giving her a “fair share” of
daily work assignments (claim 1) and placing her on an OPS plan (claim 2). Believing that was
being forced to retire, Complainant submitted retirement paperwork on July 27, 2021.

On August 2, 2021, the Agency began its EEO investigation into the formal complaint.
Complainant informed the investigator that she had received a Proposal to Terminate , and that

“overwhelming [number of] daily tasks” (claim 1) and placing her on an OPS plan (claim 2).

By memorandum dated August 6, 2021, the Supervisor notified C omplainant that he had made
the decision to terminate her employment with the Agency effective August 6, 2021. However,
the Supervisor sent Complainant an email afterward to inform her that he rescinded his decision
because she filed r etirement pape rwork in July. Complainant’s representative forwarded the
memorandum and email to the investigator and reiterated that the Agency’s actions had “forced”
Complainant into “involuntary retirement.”

Agency accepted Complainant’s constructive discharge claim as part of her original complaint or
as an amendment to it. Therefore, it does not appear as part of the report of investigation.

not request an EEOC hearing within the time frame provided in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the
Agency issued a final decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b) , with appeal rights to this
Commission. The decision concluded that no discrimination was established as alleged . The
Agency’s final decision did not address Complainant’s constructive discharge claim.

statement with her appeal.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Although Complainant’s retirement from the Agency was not effective at the time she filed her
formal EEO complaint, on the face of that complaint, Complainant alleged that she had received
“threats of termination,” and that management had done “any and everything within their power
to force [her] into retirement. ” In an attachment to her complaint, she reiterated “management
staff has left me with no other recourse, other than to concede to being forced out of my position
and into retirement! ” Once the Agency ’s investigation of her complaint was underway,
Complainant notified the investigator that she had been served with a notice of proposed removal
and that she believed she was being set up for a “ forced retirement.” The record shows that the
proposal to remove Complainant was rescinded once she initiated the retirement process.
However, despite Complainant’s repeated and clear allegations of a discriminatory constructive
discharge, the Agency did not accept the claim as an amendmen t to her original complaint , did
not investigate the claim , and did not address it in its final decision. The Agency erred in not
doing so. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.106(d) provides that a complainant may amend a complaint at any
time prior to the conclusion of the inves tigation to include issues or claims like or related to
those raised in the complaint. Here, the constructive discharge claim, which Complainant
expressly raised during the EEO investigation, was clearly like or re lated to the issues raised in
her original complaint and should have been accepted by the Agency as an amendment and
investigated.

determined that the final agency decision should be vacated, and the c omplaint should be
remanded to the A gency for a supplemental investigation on the constructive discharge claim

from an action that is appealable to the Merit Systems Protection Board (M SPB). See 29 C.F.R.

include appeal rights to the MSPB when it issues its new final decision on this matter.

specifically addressed herein, the Agency’s final decision is VACATED and the complaint is
REMANDED for further processing in accordance with the Order below.

the constructive discharge claim within ninety (90) calendar days of the date this decision

DECISION

On April 26, 2022, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s
April 11, 2022, final decision concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging employment discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964
(Title VII), as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. For the following reasons, the Commission
AFFIRMS the Agency’s final decision.

BACKGROUND

During the relevant time , Complainant worked as a Postal Support Employee at the Agency’s
O'Fallon Post Office in O'Fallon, Missouri. Supervisor Customer Service (Supervisor) was his
first-line supervisor. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 114. Acting Postmaster (Postmaster) was in
charge of the installation where Complainant worked. ROI at 98.

On November 2, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency
discriminated against him on the bases of race (African -American), sex (male), and in reprisal
for prior protected EEO activity under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 when, on June
11, 2021, he was not allowed to work Saturdays and thereafter his hours were reduced.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission Administrative Judge (AJ). When Complainant did not request a
hearing within the time frame provide d in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.108(f), the Agency issued a final
decision pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.110(b).

The Agency concluded that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected him to
discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

On appe al, Complainant offers conclusory statement s arguing his points. In addition,
Complainant asserts that, at the time he received the ROI, he did not like either the hearing
option or the final decision option, so he did not select one. He admits that he was notified by the
Agency that, if he did not select either option, the Agency would issue a final decision. He
contends that he would now like to have a hearing before an AJ. He also notes that, despite his
request, he has not been provided a paper copy of the investigative file.

The Agency did not submit a brief in opposition to the appeal.

ANALYSIS AND FINDINGS

Preliminary Matters

To the extent Complainant argues that he should be afforded a hearing at this time, despite not
requesting one upon receipt of the ROI, the Commission does not agree. EEOC regulations
specify that a complainant shall request a hearing within 30 days of receipt of the investigative
file from the Agency. 29 C.F.R. §§ 1614.108(f), 1614.110(b). Complainant states that he di d not
like either the hearing or the final decision option at the time that the investigative file was
presented to him. The Commission finds that Complainant has not provided any good cause as to
why he could not request a hearing within 30 days of receiving the investigative file. Therefore,
his request for a hearing is untimely and denied.

Similarly, there is no dispute that Complainant received the investigative file. Rather, he
expresses that he did not receive it in paper form. The Commission has he ld that the
Complainant is entitled to the investigative file, but not, necessarily, in his preferred format.
Christine G. v. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., EEOC Appeal No. 2020001284 (Aug. 9, 2021).

Standard of Review

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, pursuant to 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.110(b), the Agency's decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.405(a). See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part
1614, at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015) (explaining that the de novo standard of review
“requires that the Commission examine the record without regard to the factual and legal
determinations of the previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents,

2022002894

3
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and r elevant submissions of the
parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record and
its interpretation of the law”).

A claim of disparate treatment based on indirect evidence is examined under the three -part
analysis first enunciated in McDonnell Douglas Corporation v. Green, 411 U.S. 792 (1973). For
Complainant to prevail, they must first establish a prima facie case of discrimination by
presenting facts that, if unexplained, reasonably give rise to an inference of discrimination, i.e.,
that a prohibited consideration was a factor in the adverse employment action. McDonnell
Douglas, 411 U.S. at 802; Furnco Construction Corp. v. Waters , 438 U.S. 567 (1978). The
burden then shifts to the Agency to articulate a legit imate, nondiscriminatory reason for its
actions. Tex. Dep’t of Cmty. Aff. v. Burdine , 450 U.S. 248, 253 (1981). Once the Agency has
met its burden, Complainant bears the ultimate responsibility to persuade the fact finder by a
preponderance of the evidence that the Agency acted on the basis of a prohibited reason. St.
Mary’s Honor Ctr. v. Hicks, 509 U.S. 502 (1993).

Assuming, arguendo, that Complainant established a prima facie case of disparate treatment, we
find that the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions. Supervisor
and Postmaster averred that Complainant’s position was never scheduled to work on Saturdays;
he was only hired to work on Sundays and holidays. ROI at 142- 43, 158. Supervisor and
Postmaster explained t hat due to the contractual “pecking order,” in order for Complainant to
work on Saturdays, the Agency would be required to call in individuals to work that they did not
need in order to allow Complainant to work. ROI at 143, 158. Postmaster said that the A gency
did not need Complainant to work on Saturdays and it would be too costly for the Agency to
allow him to do so. ROI at 144.

Having found that the Agency provided legitimate, nondiscriminatory reasons for their actions ,
we now turn to Complainant to provide evidence that the Agency’s asserted reasons were merely
pretext for discrimination. Upon review, we find that he has not. Complainant relies upon his
own opinions and beliefs as evidence of discrimination. A complainant’s generalized testimony
alleging a subjective belief that a particular action was motivated by discrimination is
insufficient to show pretext. See Perry v. Dep’t of Hous. & Urban Dev., EEOC Appeal No.
01A54957 (Jan. 4. 2006).

In light of the above, we find that Complainant has not proven that he was discriminated against
as alleged.

CONCLUSION

Based on a thorough review of the record and the contentions on appeal, including those not
specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s decision.

pretext for discrimination. Upon review, we find that he has not. Complainant relies upon his

alleging a subjective belief that a particular action was motivated by discrimination is
insufficient to show pretext. See Perry v. Dep’t of Hous. & Urban Dev., EEOC Appeal No.
01A54957 (Jan. 4. 2006).

as alleged.

specifically addressed herein, we AFFIRM the Agency’s decision.

bases, we nevertheless determine t hat the Agency articulated legitimate, nondiscriminatory
reasons for not selecting Complainant for the temporary HMEM positions.

selecting official for the temporary promotions at issue. Supervisor reviewed and ultimately
selected three individuals, two a s HMEMs and one as HMEM Leader on a temporary 120-day
position. All three candidates were outside Complainant’s protected class (White, under 40 years
old, no prior EEO activity).

wished to be considered. Supervisor stated he never considered any of the candidates’ race, age,
or EEO activity in his decision , and that he solely considered the matrix criteria for the
temporary positions. In reviewing the resumes, Supervisor scored candidates based on the matrix
and whether their resumes showed r elevant experience in accordance wi th the requirements of
the WG-5803-11 Dyno Tester Leader or a WL -5803-11 Dyno Tester positions. Of the five
candidates, Complainant scored fourth highest. A r eview of the three candidates selected shows

experience, and lacked details pertaining to troubleshooting or diagnosing engines tested.

impermissible discrimination.

assertion that the t hat the three selectees were chosen out of favoritism as they are friends with
Supervisor, undermines any claim that the non-selection was motivated by a raised basis.

Agency No. HS-TSA-00724-2014

DECISION ON REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION

Complainant requested that the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or
Commission) reconsider its decision in Jamey M. v. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., EEOC Appeal No.
2022001484 (June 8, 2023). EEOC Regulations provide that the Commission may, in its
discretion, grant a request to reconsider any previous Commission decision issued pursuant to 29
C.F.R. § 1614.405(a), where the requesting party demonstrates that: (1) the appellate decision
involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or law; or (2) the appellate decision
will have a substantial impact on the policies, practices, or operations of the agency. See 29
C.F.R. § 1614.405(c).

BACKGROUND

During the relevant period, Complainant worked as a Senior Federal Air Marshal (FAM), SV -
1801-I-00, for the Federal Air Marshal Service at the Agency’s Field Office in Charlotte, North
Carolina.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2023003972

2
On March 21, 2014, Complainant filed an equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint
alleging that the Agency discriminated against him based on race (Caucasian), sex (male),
disability (learning disability), age ( born in 1967), and in reprisal for prior protected EEO
activity when, on January 3, 2014, and continuing, Complainant learned that he was being paid a
lower salary than his coworkers, who were performing the same duties as him.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of his right to request a hearing before an EEOC
Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant requested a hearing and also moved for class
certification of his complaint. After the AJ denied Complainant’s request for class certification,
the Commission vacated th e AJ’s decision and remanded the complaint to allow for
precertification discovery and/or further clarification on Complainant’s class claims. See Devon
H. v. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., EEOC Appeal No. 0120152087 (Jan. 26, 2017), request for
recons. denied, EEOC Request No. 0520170354 (Aug. 10, 2017) . However, Complainant
subsequently withdrew his requests for a hearing and for class certification. T he AJ therefore
issued an order dis missing the hearing request and class complaint and directed the Agency to
issue a final decision on the merits of Complainant’s individual complaint.

The Agency issued a final decision finding no discrimination. Complainant appealed the
Agency’s final decision to the Commission. In Devon H. v. Dep’t of Homeland Sec., EEOC
Appeal No. 2020004286 (Oct. 6, 2021), we vacated the Agency’s final decision and remanded
the matter to the Agency for a supplemental investigation regarding one of the comparat ive
employees (FAM1) Complainant had named as receiving higher pay than Complainant. We
ordered the Agency to obtain “[a]ny relevant evidence concerning [FAM1]’s professional
experiences, qualifications, and salary history prior to joining the Agency” and “[a]ffidavits from
all management and/or human resources official(s) involved in setting the initial salaries of
Complainant and [FAM1].” The Agency issued a new final decision on January 6, 2022, based
on the evidence in both the original and supplemental reports of investigation. The Agency
again found no discrimination, and Complainant appealed the new final Agency decision to the
Commission. On appeal, w e affirmed the Agency’s final decision finding no discrimination .
Complainant then filed the instant request for reconsideration.

In our prior decision affirming the Agency’s January 6, 2022 final order, we found that
Complainant had e stablished a prima facie case under the Equal Pay Act (EPA) of 1963, as
amended, 29 U.S.C. § 206(d) et seq. We also assumed that Complainant established a prima
facie case of disparate treatment under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII), as
amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq., Section 501 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973
(Rehabilitation Act), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 791 et seq., and the Age Discrimination in
Employment Act (ADEA) of 1967 (ADEA), as amended, 29 U.S.C. § 621 et seq. Complainant
named three comparative employees who were earning more pay than he did for the same job—
FAM1, FAM2, and FAM3. FAM1 and FAM3 were female and were the only comparative
employees considered for the EPA analysis . FAM2 was male and was considered, along with
FAM1 and FAM2, as part of the disparate treatment analysis.

2023003972

3
With regard to the EPA, our prior decision found that the difference in pay between the female
comparatives (FAM1 and FAM3) and Complainant was based on a factor other than sex.
Complainant and all three comparatives were originally hired as FAM s by the Department of
Transportation’s Federal Aviation Authority (FAA) , but they were soon transferred to the
Agency (Department of Homeland Security) upon its creation in November 2002. At the time of
their transfer to the Agency, the Agency maintained their FAM salaries as established by the
FAA. The FAA had determined the FAM initial salaries based on the new employees’ prior
federal salaries. Prior to becoming a F AM with the FAA in June 2002, Complainant made
$38,758 as a Detention Enforcement Officer with the Department of Justice , where he had
worked before becoming a FAM . FAM3 came directly to FAA from the Department of the
Treasury (U.S. Secret Service), where she had made $50,737.
2 FAM1 had worked for the U.S.
Immigration and Naturalization Service with a salary of $67,031 until she left to work at a state
agency for less than a year before becoming a FAM with the FAA. As a result of their respective
prior federal salaries, Complainant’s starting salary as a FAM was lower than the female
comparatives (as well as FAM2 ). Complainant and the comparatives all received subsequent
promotions and in-position increases that were proportional to their starting salaries.

Analyzing the EPA claim, o ur prior decision concluded that the Agency had proven its
affirmative defense under the EPA because any pay disparity between Complainant and the
female comparatives was the result of their beginning employment at the FAA at different rates
of pay based on their prior federal salaries, which is a factor other than sex. We further noted
that there was n o argument made that Complainant’s or the comparatives’ prior salaries before
joining the FAA or the Agency was the result of discrimination.

Analyzing Complainant’s claim under a disparate treatment framework, we found that the
Agency articulated a legit imate, nondiscriminatory reason for the pay disparity between
Complainant and the three comparatives, namely that it arose from initial salary disparities when
they entered the Federal Air Marshal Service with the FAA in 2002, which were based on each
employee’s varied federal experience prior to becoming FAMs. As such, the “built -in”

DISMISSAL OF APPEAL

Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC or
Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. § 1614.403(a), from the Agency’s January 25, 2023, final
order concerning his equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging employment
discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII), as amended,
42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. For the reasons set forth below, the Commission DISMISSED this
appeal from the Agency’s final order.

ISSUE PRESENTED

An EEOC Administrative Judge issued a decision by summary judgment concluding
Complainant failed to establish discrimination occurred as alleged, which has been adopted by
the Agency in its final order . The issue presented here is w hether Complainant’s appeal of that
final order should be dismissed because th is matter has already been resolved in the Agency’ s
negotiated grievance process.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace Complainant’s name
when the decision is published to non-parties and the Commission’s website.

2023002099

2
BACKGROUND

During the period at issue , Complainant worked for the Agency as a Maintenance Me chanic in
Cleveland, Ohio.

On November 26, 2019, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the Agency
discriminated against him based on race (African American), sex (male), and in reprisal for prior
protected EEO activity (filing his own EEO complaints and representing other employees in
EEO matters) when:

1. Complainant was denied training opportunities.

2. On or around August 8, 13, 14, 2019, and other unspecified dates, he was
denied higher level and preferred assignments.
3. On or around August 8, 13, 14, 2019, and other unspecified dates, he was
denied overtime.
4. He was made to work alone and not provided with assistance.
5. He was not given an air-conditioned vehicle to drive unlike his co-worker.

After the investigation into the claims , the Agency provided Complainant with a copy of the
report of investigation and notice of hi s right to request a hearing before an EEOC
Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a hearing.

On October 28, 2022, the Agency filed a Motion for Summary Judgment (Agency’s Motion).
Therein, the Agency found that Complainant failed to e stablish a prima facie case of reprisal.
Agency’s Motion at 14. I n its Motion , the Agency also found that it articulated legitimate,
nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish were pretext for
discrimination and/or re taliation. The Agency also noted that claim (3) was settled in the
grievance process.

Complainant filed a re sponse to the Agency’s Motion. Complainant discussed the merits of his
claims and reiterated that he was subjected to discrimination and/or retaliation. Regarding claim
(5), Complainant clarified that he was alleging that a va n was assigned to a white employee
while it should have been assigned to him , based on past practice. Complainant also submitted
various documents pertaining to grievances he filed alleging that he was subjected to disparate
treatment.

Over Complainant's objections, the AJ assigned to the case granted the Agency’s October 28,
2022 motion for a decision without a hearing and issued a decision by summary judgment in
favor of the Agency on January 18, 2023. The AJ adopted the Agency’s analysis in its Motion.

2023002099

3
The Agency subsequently issued a final order adopting the AJ’s finding that Complainant failed
to prove that the Agency subjected him to discrimination as alleged.

The instant appeal followed.

CONTENTIONS ON APPEAL

Complainant does not submit a statement or brief in support of the appeal.

In response, the Agency requests that we affirm its final action implementing the AJ’s decision
without a hearing. The Agency reiterates its reasoning set forth in its Motion for a Decision
Without a Hearing.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

In rendering this appellate decision we must scrutinize the AJ’s legal and factual conclusions,
and the Agency’s final order adopting them, de novo. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a) (stating that
a “decision on an appeal from an Agency’s final action shall be based on a de novo review . . .”);
see also Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO
MD-110), at Chap. 9, § VI.B. ( Aug. 5, 2015) (providing that an administrative judge’s
determination to issue a decision without a hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed
de novo). This essentially means that we should look at this case with fresh eyes. In other
words, we are free to accept (if accurate) or reject (if erroneous) the AJ’s, and Agency’s, factual
conclusions and legal analysis – including on the ultimate fact of whether intentional
discrimination occurred, and on the legal issue of whether any federal empl oyment
discrimination statute was violated. See id. at Chapter 9, § VI.A. (explaining that the de novo
standard of review “requires that the Commission examine the record without regard to the
factual and legal determinations of the previous decision make r,” and that EEOC “review the
documents, statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and relevant submissions
of the parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the Commission’s own assessment of the record
and its interpretation of the law”).

ANALYSIS

The Commission’s regulations allow an AJ to issue a decision without a hearing upon finding
that there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g). EEOC’s decision
without a hearing regulation follows the summary judgment pr ocedure from federal court. Fed.
R. Civ. P. 56. The U.S. Supreme Court held summary judgment is appropriate where a judge
determines no genuine issue of material fact exists under the legal and evidentiary standards.
Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc., 477 U.S. 242, 255 (1986). In ruling on a summary judgment
motion, the judge is to determine whether there are genuine issues for trial, as opposed to
weighing the evidence. Id. at 249.

2023002099

4
At the summary judgment stage, the judge must believe the non- moving party’s evidence and
must draw justifiable inferences in the non -moving party’s favor. Id. at 255. A “genuine issue of
fact” is one that a reasonable judge could find in favor for the non-moving party. Celotex v.
Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322-23 (1986); Oliver v. Digital Equip. Corp., 846 F.2d 103, 105 (1st Cir.
1988). A “material” fact has the potential to affect the outcome of a case.

Here, the AJ found that claim (3) was settled in the grievance process and addressed the
remainder of the claims on the merits . We find, however, that the record reflects that all the
claims at issue in the instant EEO complaint were settled during the grievance process. During
the EEO investigation, Complainant acknowledged filing grievances pertaining to the claims set
forth in his EEO complaint. Report of Investigation (ROI) at 65, 70, 74, 78, 97. The record also
contains handwritten statements pertaining to Complainant’s grievances signed by Complainant
which were submitted as part of the record while this matter was pending be fore the EEOC AJ.
2
Complainant, in his handwritten statements supporting his grievances, asserted that he was being
treated differently than white employees. Complainant also submitted to the AJ a list of potential
witnesses to testify at the EEOC hearin g, including named union officials to testify about the
grievances he filed.
3 Complainant’s Pre-hearing Statement.

Complainant submitted, in response to the Agency’s Motion for Summary Judgment, a copy of

nondiscriminatory reasons for its actions which Complainant failed to establish were pretext for

DECISION ON REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION

Complainant timely requested that the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission) reconsider its decision in EEOC Appeal No.

ISSUE PRESENTED

Whether Complainant’s request for reconsideration of EEOC Appeal No.
2023000533 meets the criteria detailed in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c)?

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Health Care Technician
at the Agency’s Medical Center in Hines, Illinois.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace
Complainant’s name when the decision is published to non-parties and the

 2 2024003320

On December 16, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against her on the bases of disability (PTSD, major
depressive disorder, anxiety, and panic disorder) and in reprisal for prior
protected EEO activity when:

1. From March 2, 2021 to September 23, 2021, she was denied
leave.

2. On May 7, 2021, May 8, 2021, and August 28, 2021, she
received Notice of Absent without Leave (AWOL) Order to
Return to Duty Letters;

3. On May 11, 2021, the Human Resources Specialist told her
that he did not know where her faxed medical documents were;

4. On May 11, 2021, she was denied a reasonable
accommodation;

5. Since August 31, 2021, the Chief of Surgery and Mental Health
often mentioned to her about how much time she had taken
off;

6. On August 29, 2021, she was assigned to work in area 2N;

7. On August 30, 2021, she was ordered to attend New Employee
Orientation training beginning August 31, 2021;

8. On August 31, 2021, her trainers commented on how much
time she had taken off;

9. From September 1, 2021 to September 13, 2021, she was
marked late on several days;

10. From September 24, 2021 to October 8, 2021, she was
denied leave;

11. On September 30, 2021, she was threatened with an
administrative suspension;

12. On October 26, 2021, her Proposed Removal Letter included
false and inaccurate information;

 3 2024003320

13. On November 5, 2021, she received another copy of the
same Proposed Removal letter she received the day prior;

14. On November 9, 2021, during a meeting with the Directory
and an Employee Relations Specialist, she was asked twice,
“You’ve been gone for thirteen months?”;

15. On several dates, her payroll and timekeeping hours were
incorrect or had errors; and

16. Effective November 27, 2021, she was removed from
federal employment.

The Agency investigated Complainant’s claims.

Upon completion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with
a copy of the Report of Investigation (ROI) and notice of the right to request
either a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge or an immediate final
decision by the Agency without a hearing. In accordance with Complainant’s
request, the Agency issued a final decision.

The final decision found no discrimination, reasoning that there was no
evidentiary link between the actions at issue and Complainant’s protected
classes. The final decision also set forth that claim (16), Complainant’s
removal claim, was a mixed claim and appealable to the Merit Systems
Protection Board (MSPB).
2

Operations (OFO).
3 OFO affirmed the Agency’s final decision finding no
discrimination. EEOC Appeal No. 2023000533 (March 25, 2024). OFO found

4

 4 2024003320

CONTENTIONS ON REQUEST

criteria for reconsideration.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

EEOC Regulations provide that the Commission may, in its discretion, grant a
request to reconsider any previous Commission decision issued pursuant to
29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a), where the requesting party demonstrates that: (1)
the appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material
fact or law; or (2) the appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the
policies, practices, or operations of the agency. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c).

ANALYSIS

We have reviewed the documents Complainant submitted as part of the
instant request. However, we determine that Complainant has provided no
persuasive reason to disturb the Commission’s prior decision. Some of the
documents submitted were part of the Report of Investigation and were
previously considered by the Commission when rendering its prior decision.
In addition, the other documents submitted by Complainant regarding her
removal also do not meet the criteria for a request for reconsideration. As set
forth above, the Agency determined Complainant’s removal claim to be a
mixed claim and provided her appeal rights to the MSPB (not the EEOC).

A request for reconsideration is not a second appeal to the Commission. Equal
Employment Opportunity Management Directive for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO
MD-110), Chap. 9 § VI.A (Aug. 5, 2015); see, e.g., Lopez v. Dep't of Agric.,
EEOC Request No. 0520070736 (Aug. 20, 2007). Rather, a reconsideration
request is an opportunity to demonstrate that the appellate decision involved
a clearly erroneous interpretation of material fact or law, or will have a
substantial impact on the policies, practices, or operations of the Agency.
Complainant has not done so here.

 5 2024003320

CONCLUSION

After reviewing the previous decision and the entire record, the Commission
finds that the request fails to meet the criteria of 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c),
and it is the decision of the Commission to deny the request. The decision in
EEOC Appeal No. 2023000533 remains the Commission's decision. There is
no further right of administrative appeal on the decision of the Commission on
this request.

DECISION ON REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION

Complainant timely requested that the Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission (EEOC or Commission) reconsider its decision in EEOC Appeal No.
2023000533 (March 25, 2024).

ISSUE PRESENTED

Whether Complainant’s request for reconsideration of EEOC Appeal No.
2023000533 meets the criteria detailed in 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c)?

BACKGROUND

During the period at issue, Complainant worked as a Health Care Technician
at the Agency’s Medical Center in Hines, Illinois.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace
Complainant’s name when the decision is published to non-parties and the
Commission’s website.

 2 2024003320

On December 16, 2021, Complainant filed an EEO complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against her on the bases of disability (PTSD, major
depressive disorder, anxiety, and panic disorder) and in reprisal for prior
protected EEO activity when:

1. From March 2, 2021 to September 23, 2021, she was denied
leave.

2. On May 7, 2021, May 8, 2021, and August 28, 2021, she
received Notice of Absent without Leave (AWOL) Order to
Return to Duty Letters;

3. On May 11, 2021, the Human Resources Specialist told her
that he did not know where her faxed medical documents were;

4. On May 11, 2021, she was denied a reasonable
accommodation;

5. Since August 31, 2021, the Chief of Surgery and Mental Health
often mentioned to her about how much time she had taken
off;

6. On August 29, 2021, she was assigned to work in area 2N;

7. On August 30, 2021, she was ordered to attend New Employee
Orientation training beginning August 31, 2021;

8. On August 31, 2021, her trainers commented on how much
time she had taken off;

9. From September 1, 2021 to September 13, 2021, she was
marked late on several days;

10. From September 24, 2021 to October 8, 2021, she was
denied leave;

11. On September 30, 2021, she was threatened with an
administrative suspension;

12. On October 26, 2021, her Proposed Removal Letter included
false and inaccurate information;

 3 2024003320

13. On November 5, 2021, she received another copy of the
same Proposed Removal letter she received the day prior;

14. On November 9, 2021, during a meeting with the Directory
and an Employee Relations Specialist, she was asked twice,
“You’ve been gone for thirteen months?”;

15. On several dates, her payroll and timekeeping hours were
incorrect or had errors; and

16. Effective November 27, 2021, she was removed from
federal employment.

The Agency investigated Complainant’s claims.

Upon completion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with
a copy of the Report of Investigation (ROI) and notice of the right to request
either a hearing before an EEOC Administrative Judge or an immediate final
decision by the Agency without a hearing. In accordance with Complainant’s
request, the Agency issued a final decision.

The final decision found no discrimination, reasoning that there was no
evidentiary link between the actions at issue and Complainant’s protected
classes. The final decision also set forth that claim (16), Complainant’s
removal claim, was a mixed claim and appealable to the Merit Systems
Protection Board (MSPB).
2

Complainant filed an appeal with the Commission’s Office of Federal
Operations (OFO).
3 OFO affirmed the Agency’s final decision finding no
discrimination. EEOC Appeal No. 2023000533 (March 25, 2024). OFO found

discrimination and/or retaliation.
4

2 Based on the Agency’s determination that claim (16) was a mixed claim and
the Agency instructing Complainant that she could appeal this matter to the
MSPB, our prior decision did not address claim (16).

3 Complainant did not submit a statement or brief in support of her appeal.

4 The prior decision set forth that Complainant had withdrawn claim (4).

criteria for reconsideration.

STANDARD OF REVIEW

EEOC Regulations provide that the Commission may, in its discretion, grant a
request to reconsider any previous Commission decision issued pursuant to
29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(a), where the requesting party demonstrates that: (1)
the appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of material
fact or law; or (2) the appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the
policies, practices, or operations of the agency. See 29 C.F.R. § 1614.405(c).

We have reviewed the documents Complainant submitted as part of the
instant request. However, we determine that Complainant has provided no
persuasive reason to disturb the Commission’s prior decision. Some of the

DECISION

On October 22, 2024, Complainant filed an appeal with the Equal Employment
Opportunity Commission (EEOC or Commission), pursuant to 29 C.F.R. §
1614.403(a), from the Agency’s October 3, 2024, final order concerning her
equal employment opportunity (EEO) complaint alleging employment
discrimination in violation of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VII),
as amended, 42 U.S.C. § 2000e et seq. For the following reasons, the
Commission AFFIRMS the Agency’s final order.

At the time of events giving rise to this complaint, Complainant worked as a
Driving Safety Instructor at the Agency’s Norfolk Processing and Distribution
Center in Norfolk, Virginia.

1 This case has been randomly assigned a pseudonym which will replace
Complainant’s name when the decision is published to non- parties and the
Commission’s website.

 2025000307

2
On April 29, 2024, Complainant filed a formal complaint alleging that the
Agency discriminated against her on the basis of reprisal for prior protected
EEO activity when: On or around January 26, 2024, she was not selected for
two (2) supervisory positions in Logistics Operations.

Complainant stated that she was retaliated against for whistleblower activities
when she was not selected for two supervisory positions in Logistics
Operations even though she insisted she was the best qualified candidate.
See Report of Investigation (ROI) at 71-72. The Transportation Manager who
was the selecting official for both positions asserted that she was not aware
of Complainant’s whistleblower activities at the time but explain ed that she
interviewed all the candidates recommended by the review committee and
decided that the selectees were better qualified. See ROI at 86-88; 90-92;
95. Attendance, experience and interview answers of the candidates were
considered.

At the conclusion of the investigation, the Agency provided Complainant with
a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing
before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a
hearing before an AJ.

The AJ assigned to the case determined sua sponte that the complaint did not
warrant a hearing and issued a Notice of Intent to Issue a Decision Without a
Hearing to which the Agency responded. The AJ issued a decision by summary
judgment in favor of the Agency, finding no discrimination.

The Agency subsequently issued a final order fully implementing the AJ’s
finding that Complainant failed to prove that the Agency subjected her to
discrimination as alleged. The instant appeal followed.

As this is an appeal from a decision issued without a hearing, the Agency's
decision is subject to de novo review by the Commission. 29 C.F.R.
§ 1614.405(a). See Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive for
29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD- 110), at Chap. 9, § VI.A. (Aug. 5, 2015)
(explaining that the de novo standard of review “requires that the Commission
examine the record without regard to the factual and legal determinations of
the previous decision maker,” and that EEOC “review the documents,
statements, and testimony of record, including any timely and relevant
submissions of the parties, and . . . issue its decision based on the
Commission’s own assessment of the record and its interpretation of the
law”); see also EEO MD-110, at Chap. 9, § VI.B. (Aug. 5, 2015) (providing

 2025000307

3
that an administrative judge’s determination to issue a decision without a
hearing, and the decision itself, will both be reviewed de novo).

The Commission’s regulations allow an AJ to grant summary judgment when
they find that there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. §
1614.109(g). An issue of fact is “genuine” if the evidence is such that a
reasonable fact finder could find in favor of the non-moving party. Celotex v.
Catrett, 477 U.S. 317, 322- 23 (1986); Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. , 477
U.S. 242, 247-49 (1986). A fact is “material” if it has the potential to affect
the outcome of the case. Id. When considering summary judgment, facts and
inferences must be viewed in the light most favorable to the non -moving
party. See Ricci v. DeStefano, 557 U.S. 557, 586 (2009).

To successfully oppose a decision by summary judgment, a complainant must
identify, with specificity, facts in dispute either within the record or by
producing further supporting evidence and must further establish that such
facts are material under applicable law. 29 C.F.R. § 1614.109(g)(2); Celotex,
477 U.S. at 322-24; see also EEO MD-110, at Chap. 7, § III.E. Such a dispute
would indicate that a hearing is necessary to produce evidence to support a
finding that the Agency was motivated by discriminatory animus. Here,
however, Complainant has failed to establish such a dispute. We find that the
AJ properly determined that there are no genuine issues of material fact in
dispute and therefore, h is issuance of a decision without a hearing was
appropriate.

We find that Complainant did not establish that she was subjected to reprisal.
To begin with, we note that Complainant acknowledged that she did not have
any prior EEO activity but that her protected activity was filing a whistleblower
complaint. However , whistleblower activity does not constitute protected
activity under the EEO statutes and therefore, such claims of whistleblower
retaliation do not fall within the Commission’s jurisdiction. See Brittany C. v.
Dep’t of State, EEOC Appeal No. 2019005790 (March 13, 2020). Moreover,
to the extent that Complainant argues on appeal that her non-selections were
also due to nepotism, we note that allegations of nepotism do not constitute
a violation of the EEO statutes. See Garrett W. v. U.S. Postal Serv., EEOC
Appeal No. 0120173051 (Oct. 30, 2018) (“Nepotism, does not identify a
protected class under EEOC regulations, and therefore cannot be the basis for
an actionable claim of discrimination.”); Sierra -Barber v. Dep't of Interior,
EEOC Appeal No. 0120055126 (Jan. 31, 2007) (allegations of nepotism and
favoritism do not violate EEO statutes). Finally, while Complainant clearly
believes that her non -selections were unfair, there is simply no evidence to
support her assertions.

 2025000307

4
It is well-settled that it is not within our jurisdiction to guarantee fairness in
every employment decision; we are only empowered to ensure that an
employment decision is not premised upon unlawful discriminatory animus, of
which there is simply no evidence here. See Remona P. v. Dep’t of State ,
EEOC Appeal No. 2021002652 (Aug. 2, 2022).

Having thoroughly reviewed the record, and construing any inferences raised
by the undisputed facts in favor of Complainant, we find that a reasonable
fact-finder could not find in Complainant’s favor. Upon careful review of the
AJ’s decision and the evidence of record, as well as the parties’ arguments on
appeal, we conclude that the AJ correctly determined that the preponderance
of the evidence did not establish that Complainant was discriminated against
by the Agency as alleged.

Accordingly, we AFFIRM the Agency’s final order implementing the AJ’s
decision.

RECONSIDERATION (M0425)
The Commission may, in its discretion, reconsider this appellate decision if
Complainant or the Agency submits a written request that contains arguments
or evidence that tend to establish that:
1. The appellate decision involved a clearly erroneous interpretation of

2. The appellate decision will have a substantial impact on the policies,
practices, or operations of the agency.
Requests for reconsideration must be filed with EEOC’s Office of Federal
Operations (OFO) within thirty (30) calendar days of receipt of this
decision. If the party requesting reconsideration elects to file a statement or
brief in support of the request, that statement or brief must be filed
together with the request for reconsideration . A party shall have
twenty (20) calendar days from receipt of another party’s request for
reconsideration within which to submit a brief or statement in opposition. See
29 C.F.R. § 1614.405; Equal Employment Opportunity Management Directive
for 29 C.F.R. Part 1614 (EEO MD-110), at Chap. 9 § VII.B (Aug. 5, 2015).
Complainant should submit their request for reconsideration, and any
statement or brief in support of their request, via the EEOC Public Portal, which
can be found at https://publicportal.eeoc.gov/Portal/Login.aspx.

 2025000307

5
Alternatively, Complainant can submit their request and arguments to the
Director, Office of Federal Operations, Equal Employment Opportunity
Commission, via regular mail addressed to P.O. Box 77960, Washington, DC
20013, or by certified mail addressed to 131 M Street, NE, Washington, DC
20507. In the absence of a legible postmark, a complainant’s request to
reconsider shall be deemed timely filed if OFO receives it by mail within five
days of the expiration of the applicable filing period. See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.604.
An agency’s request for reconsideration must be submitted in digital format
via the EEOC’s Federal Sector EEO Portal (FedSEP). See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.403(g). Either party’s request and/or statement or brief in opposition
must also include proof of service on the other party, unless Complainant files
their request via the EEOC Public Portal, in which case no proof of service is
required.
Failure to file within the 30 -day time period will result in dismissal of the
party’s request for reconsideration as untimely, unless extenuating
circumstances prevented the timely filing of the request. Any supporting
documentation must be submitted together with the request for
reconsideration. The Commission will consider requests for reconsideration
filed after the deadline only in very limited circumstances. See 29 C.F.R. §
1614.604(f).
COMPLAINANT’S RIGHT TO FILE A CIVIL ACTION (S0124)

You have the right to file a civil action in an appropriate United States District
Court within ninety (90) calendar days from the date that you receive this
decision. If you file a civil action, you must name as the defendant in the
complaint the person who is the official Agency head or department head,
identifying that person by their full name and official title. Failu re to do so
may result in the dismissal of your case in court. “Agency” or “department”
means the national organization, and not the l ocal office, facility or
department in which you work. If you file a request to reconsider and also file
a civil action, filing a civil action will terminate the administrative
processing of your complaint.

RIGHT TO REQUEST COUNSEL (Z0815)

If you want to file a civil action but cannot pay the fees, costs, or security to
do so, you may request permission from the court to proceed with the civil
action without paying these fees or costs.

 2025000307

6
Similarly, if you cannot afford an attorney to represent you in the civil action,
you may request the court to appoint an attorney for you. You must submit
the requests for waiver of court costs or appointment of an attorney
directly to the court, not the Commission. The court has the sole
discretion to grant or deny these types of requests. Such requests do not alter
the time limits for filing a civil action (please read the paragraph titled
Complainant’s Right to File a Civil Action for the specific time limits).

when she was not selected for two supervisory positions in Logistics
Operations even though she insisted she was the best qualified candidate.

interviewed all the candidates recommended by the review committee and
decided that the selectees were better qualified. See ROI at 86-88; 90-92;

considered.

a copy of the report of investigation and notice of her right to request a hearing
before an EEOC Administrative Judge (AJ). Complainant timely requested a
hearing before an AJ.

warrant a hearing and issued a Notice of Intent to Issue a Decision Without a

judgment in favor of the Agency, finding no discrimination.

they find that there is no genuine issue of material fact. 29 C.F.R. §
1614.109(g). An issue of fact is “genuine” if the evidence is such that a
reasonable fact finder could find in favor of the non-moving party. Celotex v.
